question: How does rain happen?
title: How Does Rain Happen?
summary: Follow water from sunny surfaces into clouds and back to Earth as rain.

slides.title: Water rises as vapor
slides.explanation: The Sun warms water in oceans, lakes, rivers, and puddles. Some liquid water evaporates into invisible water vapor.
slides.fun_fact: Water vapor is a gas, so you cannot see it floating in the air.
slides.narration: The Sun warms water in oceans, lakes, rivers, and puddles. Some of that liquid water becomes invisible water vapor and rises into the air.

slides.title: Cool air helps clouds form
slides.explanation: Higher in the sky, water vapor can cool and condense onto tiny particles, forming very small drops of liquid water or bits of ice.
slides.fun_fact: A cloud is made of tiny water drops or ice crystals, not water vapor alone.
slides.narration: Higher up, the air is often cooler. Water vapor changes back into tiny drops of liquid water, and many of those drops make a cloud.

slides.title: Drops grow and fall
slides.explanation: Cloud drops collide and join together. When drops grow too heavy for moving air to keep aloft, they fall as rain.
slides.fun_fact: Raindrops are shaped more like tiny hamburger buns than teardrops as they fall.
slides.narration: Tiny cloud drops bump together and grow. When a drop becomes too heavy to stay in the cloud, it falls as rain.

slides.title: The journey continues
slides.explanation: Rain may run into streams and oceans, soak into the ground, or be taken up by plants. Water keeps moving through many connected paths.
slides.fun_fact: Plants return some water to the air through a process called transpiration.
slides.narration: Rain can flow into streams and oceans, soak into the ground, or be used by plants. Then some water evaporates again. That repeating journey is the water cycle.

question: Why is Jupiter the biggest planet?
title: Jupiter: The Biggest Planet
summary: Meet our solar system's largest planet, its striped clouds, giant storm, and four famous moons.

slides.title: A giant world
slides.explanation: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system. Its diameter is about eleven times Earth's diameter.
slides.fun_fact: If Jupiter were a hollow shell, roughly one thousand Earths could fit inside it.
slides.narration: Jupiter is the biggest planet in our solar system. It is so wide that more than ten Earths could fit side by side across it.

slides.title: Clouds instead of ground
slides.explanation: Jupiter has no solid surface like Earth's. Its visible bands are clouds moving through a deep atmosphere made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
slides.fun_fact: Jupiter spins once in about ten hours, giving it the shortest day of any planet.
slides.narration: Jupiter does not have a solid surface like Earth's. What we see from far away are thick, swirling clouds arranged in colorful bands.

slides.title: The Great Red Spot
slides.explanation: The Great Red Spot is a huge, long-lasting storm in Jupiter's atmosphere. Its size and shape change over time.
slides.fun_fact: Spacecraft images show smaller storms swirling near the Great Red Spot too.
slides.narration: One giant storm is called the Great Red Spot. People have watched it through telescopes for hundreds of years, although its shape and size change.

slides.title: Four famous moons
slides.explanation: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto are Jupiter's four largest moons. Galileo observed them with an early telescope in 1610.
slides.fun_fact: Ganymede is the largest moon in our solar system-even larger than the planet Mercury.
slides.narration: Jupiter also has many moons. Four large ones-Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto-can be seen with a small telescope or binoculars under good conditions. Which one would you explore first?

question: How do fireflies glow?
title: How Do Fireflies Glow?
summary: Discover the chemistry, patterns, and cool efficiency behind a firefly's flashing light.

slides.title: A living lantern
slides.explanation: Many fireflies make light in a special organ in their abdomen. This light made by a living thing is called bioluminescence.
slides.fun_fact: Fireflies are beetles, not flies.
slides.narration: A tiny light flashes in the dark. It is a firefly! Many fireflies make light in a special part of their bodies.

slides.title: A light-making reaction
slides.explanation: Luciferin reacts with oxygen inside light-producing cells. An enzyme called luciferase helps the reaction release energy as light.
slides.fun_fact: The names luciferin and luciferase come from a Latin word connected with light.
slides.narration: Inside that part, a substance called luciferin reacts with oxygen. An enzyme called luciferase helps the reaction happen, and light is produced.

slides.title: Patterns send signals
slides.explanation: Different firefly species use different flash rhythms. Many adults use these patterns to recognize and find mates of their own species.
slides.fun_fact: Some firefly species flash together in synchronized patterns.
slides.narration: Different kinds of fireflies flash in different patterns. The flashes help many fireflies find others of their own kind.

slides.title: Cool, efficient light
slides.explanation: Firefly light releases very little heat compared with an old-style incandescent bulb, so most of the reaction's energy becomes light.
slides.fun_fact: Firefly light may look yellow, green, or orange depending on the species.
slides.narration: Firefly light gives off very little heat compared with a light bulb. That is why this kind of living light is sometimes called cold light.

question: Do platypuses lay eggs?
title: Platypuses Lay Eggs!
summary: Meet an unusual Australian mammal that swims, lays eggs, and feeds its young milk.

slides.title: Built for freshwater
slides.explanation: Platypuses have waterproof fur, webbed feet, and a sensitive bill. They live around freshwater in eastern Australia and Tasmania.
slides.fun_fact: A platypus closes its eyes, ears, and nostrils while diving.
slides.narration: A platypus has a bill like a duck and fur like a mammal. It lives in and around freshwater in eastern Australia and Tasmania.

slides.title: A mammal that lays eggs
slides.explanation: A female platypus lays small, soft-shelled eggs and curls around them in a nesting burrow to keep them warm.
slides.fun_fact: Platypus eggs are much smaller and softer than a chicken's egg.
slides.narration: Most mammals give birth to live young. A female platypus lays eggs instead and keeps them warm in a burrow.

slides.title: Milk for hatchlings
slides.explanation: After hatching, young platypuses drink milk that comes through pores in their mother's skin. Milk is a defining mammal trait.
slides.fun_fact: A platypus mother does not have nipples; milk gathers in grooves on her skin and fur.
slides.narration: When the young hatch, their mother feeds them milk. That is one of the clues that tells us a platypus is a mammal, even though it lays eggs.

slides.title: Meet the monotremes
slides.explanation: Platypuses and echidnas belong to the monotremes, the only living group of egg-laying mammals.
slides.fun_fact: Only five living monotreme species are known: one platypus and four echidnas.
slides.narration: Platypuses belong to a small group of egg-laying mammals called monotremes. Echidnas belong to that group too. Nature does not always fit our first guesses!

question: Where do jumping spiders live?
title: Where Jumping Spiders Live
summary: Look for these tiny, sharp-eyed hunters in habitats from gardens and forests to sunny walls.

slides.title: Neighbors around the world
slides.explanation: Jumping spiders live on every continent except Antarctica. Different species occupy plants, forests, deserts, rocky ground, and buildings.
slides.fun_fact: Scientists have described more than six thousand species of jumping spiders.
slides.narration: Jumping spiders live in many parts of the world, from gardens and forests to walls near our homes. Look closely and you might spot one watching its surroundings.

slides.title: Eyes made for looking
slides.explanation: Jumping spiders have several eyes. Their two large front eyes provide especially detailed vision that helps them judge distance.
slides.fun_fact: Some jumping spiders turn their bodies to follow an interesting object with their front eyes.
slides.narration: A jumping spider has several eyes. Its large front eyes give it especially sharp vision for a spider.

slides.title: Stalk, leap, and tether
slides.explanation: Many jumping spiders stalk prey instead of trapping it in a web. Before leaping, they attach a silk dragline that can act as a safety tether.
slides.fun_fact: A jumping spider uses changes in pressure inside its legs to help extend them for a leap.
slides.narration: Instead of catching every meal in a web, it often stalks an insect and leaps toward it. A silk safety line can help keep it from falling far.

slides.title: Watch without worry
slides.explanation: Jumping spiders are small hunters that usually avoid people. Observing one without touching or disturbing it is a good way to notice its behavior.
slides.fun_fact: Many jumping spiders communicate with movements, including waves and dances.
slides.narration: Jumping spiders are small hunters, but they do not need to scare us. Watching one from a respectful distance is a great way to notice how carefully it moves.

question: How do plants eat sunlight?
title: How Plants Eat Sunlight
summary: See how leaves use light, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar through photosynthesis.

slides.title: Light is energy, not lunch
slides.explanation: Plants do not eat sunlight as food. They capture light energy and use it to build sugar, which stores chemical energy.
slides.fun_fact: The word photosynthesis combines ideas meaning light and putting together.
slides.narration: A plant does not eat sunlight the way we eat lunch. It uses sunlight as energy to make its own food.

slides.title: Gathering the ingredients
slides.explanation: Roots absorb water from soil, while carbon dioxide enters leaves from the air. Chlorophyll in leaves captures light energy.
slides.fun_fact: Chlorophyll reflects much of the green light that reaches it, helping leaves look green.
slides.narration: Its roots take in water, and its leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air. Green material in the leaves captures light.

slides.title: Making sugar
slides.explanation: Using light energy, plants combine carbon dioxide and water to make sugars. This energy-storing process is called photosynthesis.
slides.fun_fact: Plants can join simple sugars into larger materials such as starch and cellulose.
slides.narration: With light energy, the plant combines water and carbon dioxide to make sugar. This process is called photosynthesis.

slides.title: Energy for a living world
slides.explanation: Plants use sugars to grow and power their cells, while oxygen made during photosynthesis is released. Animals gain stored energy by eating plants or plant-eating animals.
slides.fun_fact: Much of the oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from water molecules.
slides.narration: The plant uses that sugar to grow and releases oxygen into the air. Plants also become food for many animals, connecting sunlight to living things all around us.
